principles.name: Act for the global good
principles.description: Make decisions that maximize positive outcomes for humanity in the long run, even when that costs short-term gain.
evidence_signals: Weighs long-term societal impact, not only team or company metrics
Describes giving up a short-term win for a better long-term outcome
Considers people affected beyond the direct user

principles.name: Hold light and shade
principles.description: Take AI's risks seriously while also seeing its potential benefits; hold both at once.
evidence_signals: Articulates concrete risks and concrete benefits of the same technology
Avoids both hype and doom; reasons with nuance and uncertainty
Changes position when presented with good evidence

principles.name: Be good to our users
principles.description: Bring generosity and kindness to interactions with customers, policymakers, colleagues and affected communities.
evidence_signals: Shows care for users' real needs and trust
Describes treating colleagues and partners generously
Balances helpfulness with protecting users

principles.name: Ignite a race to the top on safety
principles.description: Set industry standards for trustworthy AI and show that safety and capability can go together, inspiring others to follow.
evidence_signals: Treats safety as a design requirement, not an afterthought
Raised the bar on security, privacy or safety in past work
Has thought-through views on AI safety practices and policy

principles.name: Do the simple thing that works
principles.description: Be empirical and pragmatic: prefer simple, measurable approaches that deliver impact over unnecessary complexity.
evidence_signals: Chose a simple solution and explains why it was enough
Uses experiments and data to decide
Cuts complexity that did not pay off

principles.name: Be helpful, honest, and harmless
principles.description: Operate as a high-trust, low-ego organization; communicate directly and kindly and be honest even when it is uncomfortable.
evidence_signals: Admits mistakes and uncertainty plainly
Gives or receives hard feedback directly and kindly
Credits others; low ego in disagreements

principles.name: Put the mission first
principles.description: A shared purpose, the safe transition through transformative AI, is the final arbiter of decisions.
evidence_signals: Motivation is clearly tied to the mission, not only the role or brand
Describes putting the shared goal above personal or team credit
Can engage critically with the mission and Anthropic's strategy

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a moral or ethical conflict you faced at work. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a real situation with genuine tension (privacy, misleading users, cutting a safety corner). Explain the stakes, who was affected, the options you weighed, and what you did, including raising it with the right people. Be honest about uncertainty and the cost to you. Interviewers look for principled judgment and honesty, not heroics. Pitfall: a clean story with no real trade-off.

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you had to balance delivery speed against security or safety.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out the deadline pressure and the specific risk. Show how you quantified the risk, looked for the simplest mitigation that made shipping safe (a flag, limited rollout, extra review), and who decided. Give the outcome and what you would do again. Strong answers treat safety as a requirement, not a blocker.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety
Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you received negative feedback. How did you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick feedback that stung and was at least partly right. Describe your first reaction honestly, how you sought to understand it, and the concrete change you made with evidence it stuck. Low ego and direct, kind communication are the signals. Pitfall: feedback that was really a compliment.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about shipping something you were not fully comfortable with.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain what worried you and why it shipped anyway. Show that you voiced the concern clearly, proposed mitigations, and owned the follow-up (monitoring, fixes). Reflect honestly on whether it was the right call. Anthropic interviewers value candour and judgment over a perfect record.

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you failed to deliver on a commitment.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Own it plainly: what you committed, why you missed, and when you told people. Spend most time on recovery and what you changed (estimation, scope, saying no earlier). Pitfall: blaming dependencies without your part.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a disagreement with your manager or a senior stakeholder.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a substantive issue. Show you stated your view directly with evidence, genuinely engaged with theirs, and resolved it by what best served the shared goal, whether or not you won. Describe the outcome and relationship afterwards. Low ego and mission-first reasoning are key.

sample_questions.question: Which risk from advanced AI do you think is most underrated, and why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a specific risk and argue it with reasoning and evidence, acknowledging counterarguments and uncertainty. Also note benefits you think are real. Show how the risk could be measured or mitigated and how it connects to your work. Interviewers test conviction and depth, so expect follow-ups. Pitfall: vague doom or dismissiveness.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

sample_questions.question: What ethical risks do you see in deploying autonomous AI agents, and how would you reduce them?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Identify concrete risks: unintended actions, misuse, data exposure, over-reliance, unclear accountability. Propose layered mitigations: scoped permissions, human confirmation for consequential actions, monitoring and audit logs, staged rollout, and evaluations. Weigh these against usefulness. Strong answers are specific and balanced.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

sample_questions.question: Why Anthropic specifically, and do you have any concerns about its mission or approach?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a specific, personal reason tied to the mission and to what Anthropic does differently (for example its safety research or deployment policies). Then engage honestly with a real concern or tension (such as building frontier models while warning of their risks) and how you reconcile it. Interviewers value critical thinking over flattery.

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a past project you are proud of and the key decisions you made.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the problem, users, your role, two or three key decisions with the alternatives, and the measured outcome. Highlight where you chose a simpler approach and why it was enough, and what you learned. Be ready for detailed follow-ups.
values: Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: How do you turn research findings into product requirements?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a concrete example: understanding what the research shows and its limits, translating capabilities into user value, defining requirements and evaluation criteria with researchers, and handling uncertainty with staged launches. Show respect for empirical evidence and close partnership with research.
values: Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: Design a batch inference API for a large language model.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the contract: submit many requests, poll or get notified, results within an SLA, lower price. Cover a job store, queueing, packing requests into GPU batches by length, scheduling around interactive traffic, retries, partial results, and cost accounting. Discuss throughput versus latency and fairness between customers. Start simple and scale.
values: Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: Design a token-generation service that handles around 100,000 requests per second.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Estimate GPU capacity from tokens per request and per-GPU throughput. Cover load balancing, continuous batching, KV cache memory management, streaming responses, autoscaling, admission control and priority tiers. Discuss tail latency, failure of a GPU mid-generation, and observability (utilization, queue depth). Show numbers.
values: Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: How would you distribute very large model files to thousands of machines quickly?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Compute the naive cost from a single source to show the bottleneck. Propose peer-to-peer or tree distribution, chunking with checksums, rack-aware placement, local caching, and resumable transfers. Discuss verifying integrity, rollout of new versions, and handling stragglers. Compare with object storage plus caching layers.

sample_questions.question: What is an LLM hallucination, why does it happen, and how can it be reduced?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define it as fluent output not supported by facts or provided context. Explain causes: next-token training objective, gaps in training data, pressure to answer, decoding choices. Mitigations: grounding with retrieval and citations, training to express uncertainty, evaluations that reward abstaining, and product design that shows sources. Be precise and honest about limits.

sample_questions.question: A model is found to reveal sensitive data from its training set. How do you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Treat it as an incident: contain (filters, block patterns), assess scope and affected people, notify appropriately. Then root cause: data pipeline filtering, deduplication, memorization tests. Longer term: privacy reviews, red-teaming for extraction, and evaluations before release. Balance speed with user trust.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

sample_questions.question: How would you improve an AI assistant's web app for first-time users?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define who new users are and what success looks like (first useful outcome, return within a week). Find where they struggle (blank-page problem, not knowing capabilities, trust). Propose a few ideas, prioritize one, and define metrics and guardrails. Consider safety and honesty about limits as part of the experience.

sample_questions.question: How would you set launch criteria that balance a model's helpfulness against potential harms?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define both sides measurably: helpfulness evaluations and over-refusal rates, harm evaluations by risk category and severity. Propose thresholds, red-teaming, staged rollout and monitoring, and who decides when they conflict. Explain that unhelpfulness has costs too. Strong answers are concrete and reflect holding risk and benefit together.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize capability improvements against safety improvements on a product roadmap?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Reject the false binary: show how some safety work enables capability launches and trust. Propose a framework weighing user value, risk severity and likelihood, and commitments. Give an example trade-off and your decision, plus how you would revisit it. Mission-first reasoning with clear prioritization.
values: Ignite a race to the top on safety

sample_questions.question: How would you find high-potential use cases for a new AI capability before you have usage data?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use proxies: customer interviews, early-access partners, internal dogfooding, analogous products, and the capability's evaluated strengths. Size candidate use cases by value and frequency, test quickly with prototypes, and define what signal would confirm demand. Keep it empirical and simple.
values: Do the simple thing that works

sample_questions.question: Design an AI feature for enterprise users of an AI assistant.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a specific enterprise persona and job to be done. Cover enterprise needs: admin controls, data privacy, integrations, auditability. Propose the feature, the minimum lovable version, and metrics (adoption, retention, seat expansion), with risks and mitigations.

bar_by_level.level_name: Member of Technical Staff (reported internal T4)
bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Levels are not public; everyone is titled Member of Technical Staff. Expect independent ownership of well-scoped projects.

bar_by_level.level_name: Member of Technical Staff (reported internal T5)
bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Levels not public. Expect leading significant projects with little direction and strong judgment on trade-offs.

bar_by_level.level_name: Member of Technical Staff (reported internal T6)
bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Levels not public. Expect cross-team technical leadership on critical systems or research directions.

persona.tone: Warm, thoughtful and candid; low ego and genuinely curious
persona.pace: Unhurried; leaves space for the candidate to reason aloud and admit uncertainty
persona.pushback_style: Probes the reasoning behind views with 'why do you believe that?' and 'what would change your mind?', and asks for the simplest thing that would work
persona.closing_style: Invites honest questions, including critical ones about Anthropic's mission and approach

case_style.notes: Cases are AI-specific and often turn on safety versus helpfulness trade-offs and launch criteria. Estimation is rare.

low_confidence_notes: bar_by_level: Anthropic does not publish levels; all engineers are titled Member of Technical Staff. Internal level labels (T4-T6) come from anonymous Blind posts seen in search only. No new-grad or PM levels listed.

loop_structure: round order and durations come from candidate reports and prep guides; the careers page only confirms live coding for technical roles and conversational interviews for others. The research engineer loop is less well sourced.
values_share: set to 0.35 because several reports say the culture interview is the most common rejection point; this is a judgment call.
scoring_weights: estimated; no public source gives weights.
case_style: PM case reports are few and come from one guide.
